mainTopic: The dangers of anger, and undoing serious vows (including those made with 'אלהי ישראל')
overview: This amud finishes a short story from the previous page, where the people involved had not yet crossed the Jordan. The גמרא then brings three sayings about how harmful anger is: it pushes away awareness of the שכינה, makes a person forget his learning, and shows that his sins outweigh his merits. רב אדא ברבי חנינא adds that if ישראל had not sinned and angered God, they would have received only the Torah and ספר יהושע. The גמרא then returns to vows. רבי אסי teaches that a vow made with 'אלהי ישראל' is not undone unless it rested on a false fact, and stories about רב אסי and about רב כהנא at רב יוסף's home show this strict approach. רב נחמן then rules that the הלכה is that regret is a valid opening, and that even a vow by 'אלהי ישראל' can be undone. In a story, רב סחורה cannot find an opening before רב נחמן, so he uses רב נחמן's annoyance as an opening to undo his own vow. A similar story about רבי שמעון ברבי begins, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: They were still outside ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: The last words of an answer from the previous page: the event happened before they crossed the Jordan.
steps.simpleTranslation: We had not yet crossed the Jordan.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes an answer that started on the previous page. The speaker explains that when the event happened, they had not yet crossed the Jordan River into ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question on the previous page assumed that the curse of 'an angry heart' belongs outside ארץ ישראל. The answer is that this fits, because they were still outside the land at the time. So the anger in the story matches where it happened.

phrases.english: We had not crossed the Jordan.
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from the previous page: we were still outside ארץ ישראל when this happened.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer from the previous page.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Setting the place and time of the event
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the anger in the story happened inside ארץ ישראל, where the curse of anger should not apply.
steps.terutzMaskana: It happened before they crossed the Jordan, so the curse of anger still applied there.

steps.title: An angry person ignores even the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא teaches that when someone gets angry, even the שכינה does not matter to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: Anyone who gets angry, even the Divine Presence is not important to him, as the verse says: 'The wicked, in his great anger, does not seek; all his thoughts are: There is no God.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the story was about anger, the גמרא now brings sayings about how bad anger is. רבה בר רב הונא says that an angry person stops caring even about the שכינה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse links being 'at the height of anger' with thinking 'there is no God.' So רבה בר רב הונא learns that anger blocks a person's awareness of God in that moment. This is the first of three sayings on the harm of anger.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
Anyone who gets angry,
even the Divine Presence is not important to him,
as it says: 'The wicked, in the height of his anger, does not seek;
all his thoughts are: There is no God.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא: כׇּל הַכּוֹעֵס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The story's theme of anger leads into general teachings about anger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a person is angry, even the שכינה does not matter to him.

steps.title: Anger makes a person forget his learning
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה מדיפתי says an angry person forgets what he learned and grows more foolish.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה of Difti said: An angry person forgets his learning and adds foolishness, as it says: 'For anger rests in the bosom of fools,' and it says: 'And a fool spreads out folly.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second sage gives another harm of anger. רבי ירמיה מדיפתי says anger makes a person forget his Torah learning and become more foolish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He joins two verses. The first says anger lives inside a fool, so the angry person counts as a fool. The second says a fool spreads out foolishness, so his foolishness grows and his wisdom slips away.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti said:
He forgets his learning and adds foolishness,
as it says: 'For anger rests in the bosom of fools,'
and it is written: 'And a fool spreads out folly.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה מִדִּיפְתִּי אָמַר: מְשַׁכֵּחַ תַּלְמוּדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second view on the harm caused by anger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An angry person forgets his learning and becomes more foolish.

steps.title: An angry person's sins outweigh his merits
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says it is clear that an angry person has more sins than merits.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: It is known that his sins are more than his merits, as it says: 'And a wrathful man has much transgression.'
steps.whatsHappening: A third sage adds his view. רב נחמן בר יצחק says an angry person surely has more sins than good deeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse calls the angry man 'רב פשע,' full of sin. From this רב נחמן בר יצחק learns that his sins must be more than his merits. This closes the group of three sayings about anger.
steps.whatToRemember: Three sages, three harms of anger: it pushes away awareness of the שכינה, it causes forgetting of learning and adds foolishness, and it shows that one's sins outweigh one's merits.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
It is known that his sins are more than his merits,
as it says: 'And a wrathful man has much transgression.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר: בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁעֲוֹנוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third view on the harm caused by anger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An angry person's sins are clearly more than his merits.

steps.title: Without sin, only the Torah and ספר יהושע
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא ברבי חנינא says that had ישראל not sinned, they would have received only the five books of the Torah and ספר יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא ברבי חנינא said: Had ישראל not sinned, they would have been given only the five books of the Torah and the book of יהושע, because it contains the layout of ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching connected to anger, this time God being angered by ישראל's sins. רב אדא ברבי חנינא says that without sin, the only books given would have been the Torah and ספר יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ספר יהושע would still be needed because it lays out the land and its division, which matters for all generations. The other books of נביאים came because ישראל sinned and needed to be warned. The source for this comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: if not, had it not been
the five books of the Torah

phrases.english: Rav Adda son of Rabbi Chanina said:
Had Israel not sinned,
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is in the printed גמרא, but the corrected text leaves it out. אלמלא already means 'had not.'

phrases.english: they would have been given nothing except
the five books of the Torah
and the book of Joshua alone,
because it is the layout of the Land of Israel.
phrases.notes: 'It' is ספר יהושע, which describes how the land was divided. Every generation needs that.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: אִלְמָלֵא (לֹא) חָטְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the anger theme, now about ישראל angering God.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without sin, ישראל would have received only the Torah and ספר יהושע.

steps.title: The verse behind רב אדא's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source and brings the verse 'In much wisdom is much anger.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? 'For in much wisdom is much anger.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what source supports רב אדא's teaching, and answers with a verse from קהלת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse ties 'much wisdom' to 'much anger.' This hints that much of the wisdom in the books of נביאים came because ישראל angered God. Without that anger, those extra books would not have been needed.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
'For in much wisdom is much anger.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the verse that supports רב אדא's teaching in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: רב אדא's claim that the extra books of נביאים came because of sin

steps.title: Vows made with 'אלהי ישראל' are not undone
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי rules that a vow invoking 'אלהי ישראל' is not undone, except when it was based on something that turned out to be false.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי said: We do not deal with undoing a vow made with 'the God of Israel,' except for: 'Benefit from me is קונם for my wife because she stole my purse and because she hit my son,' and then it became known that she did not steal and did not hit him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the laws of vows. רבי אסי says a חכם will not undo a vow made with the words 'אלהי ישראל,' with one exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Invoking 'אלהי ישראל' makes a vow extra serious, so a חכם does not undo it. The exception is when the husband made the vow because of something his wife supposedly did, and it turns out she never did it. Then the vow was a mistake from the start, so it can be undone.

keyTerms.meaning: we do not deal with (we do not help undo)
a word used to make something forbidden by a vow

steps.confusionAlert: The exception does not mean this vow is weaker in general. It works only because the vow rested on facts that turned out to be false, so it was a mistake from the start.
steps.whyThisMatters: This brings the sugya back from stories about anger to the laws of נדרים. It shows that even a very serious vow can be undone when it was based on a false fact.

phrases.english: Rabbi Asi said:
We do not deal with a vow of 'the God of Israel,'
phrases.notes: He means a חכם will not help undo a vow made with these words.

phrases.english: except for: 'Benefit from me is קונם for my wife'
because she stole my purse
and because she hit my son,'
and it became known that she did not steal
and that she did not hit him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי: אֵין נִזְקָקִין לֶ״אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the stories about anger and returns to the laws of undoing vows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow invoking 'אלהי ישראל' is not undone, unless it was based on a claim that turned out to be false.

steps.title: רב אסי refuses to undo a woman's vow made by אלהי ישראל
steps.stepSummary: A woman asks רב אסי to undo her vow. When she says she vowed 'by the God of Israel,' he refuses. He would have helped if she had only used a substitute name like 'מוהי.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman came to רב אסי. He asked her: 'What words did you use in your vow?' She said: 'By the God of Israel.' He said: 'If you had vowed by "מוהי," which is only a stand-in name, I would help you. But since you vowed by the God of Israel, I will not help you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows רב אסי's ruling from step 7 being used in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7, רבי אסי said a vow by 'the God of Israel' is not undone. Here we see the line he draws: a vow with a mere substitute name (כינוי) can be undone, but one using the solemn name 'God of Israel' cannot. The story backs up his rule with a real case.

keyTerms.meaning: A stand-in word people used in place of God's name when vowing
A substitute name, not the real name itself
I will attend to you, I will deal with your request

phrases.english: A certain woman who came before Rav Asi,
he said to her: With what did you vow?
She answered: By the God of Israel.
He said to her: If you had vowed by 'mohi,'
which is merely a substitute name,
I would attend to your request;
now that you did not vow by 'mohi'
but rather by the God of Israel,
I will not attend to your request.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows רב אסי's ruling from step 7 applied in an actual case.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אסי's rule that a vow by 'the God of Israel' is not undone
steps.raayaSupportSource: A story of רב אסי refusing to undo a woman's vow

steps.title: רב כהנא vows not to eat at רב יוסף's home
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף offers רב כהנא food. רב כהנא swears 'No, by the Master of all, I will not eat.' רב יוסף answers with the same words: 'No, by the Master of all, you will not eat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא visited רב יוסף's house. רב יוסף said: 'Let the master taste something.' רב כהנא said: 'No, by the Master of all, I will not taste it.' רב יוסף said back to him: 'No, by the Master of all, you will not taste it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about a serious vow made with a solemn name for God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא swore by 'the Master of all,' a very serious way to vow. רב יוסף's reply repeats the same words, which seems strange; the גמרא will ask about that in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master of all, a name for God
To taste, to eat a little

phrases.aramaic: רַב כָּהֲנָא אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רַב יוֹסֵף,
phrases.english: Rav Kahana happened to come to the home of Rav Yosef.
He said to him: Let the master taste something.
He said to him: No, by the Master of all,
I will not taste it.
He said to him: No, by the Master of all,
phrases.notes: Now רב יוסף is the one speaking, using the same words back.

phrases.english: you will not taste it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story illustrating that a vow by a solemn name of God is treated very seriously.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that a vow by a solemn name of God is not undone
steps.raayaSupportSource: The exchange between רב כהנא and רב יוסף

steps.title: Why did רב יוסף repeat the vow words?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא understands why רב כהנא said 'by the Master of all,' since he was vowing. But why would רב יוסף say it too?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for רב כהנא to say 'No, by the Master of all,' because he was making a vow. But why did רב יוסף also say 'No, by the Master of all'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask about a puzzling detail in the story and sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף was the host who wanted his guest to eat, so he had no reason to vow. His use of the same oath words needs explaining.

keyTerms.meaning: It is fine, it makes sense

phrases.english: It is understandable for Rav Kahana,
who said: 'No, by the Master of all.'
But as for Rav Yosef,
why did he say 'No, by the Master of all'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions a strange detail in the story of step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What did רב יוסף mean by repeating 'No, by the Master of all'?

steps.title: רב יוסף was quoting רב כהנא's own vow
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף was not vowing himself. He was telling רב כהנא: you said 'by the Master of all,' so now you may not eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רב יוסף meant: 'You are the one who said "No, by the Master of all." So now you cannot eat it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: רב יוסף was repeating רב כהנא's words to show him his vow now binds him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף was pointing out that a vow made with such a solemn name cannot be undone. This matches the strict view of רבי אסי from step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he was saying to him

steps.whatToRemember: Both stories (רב אסי and רב יוסף) show the strict view: a vow made with a solemn name of God stays in force.

phrases.english: This is what he was saying to him:
'No, by the Master of all' is what you said,
therefore you may not taste it.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב יוסף was quoting רב כהנא's vow back to him to show it cannot be undone.

steps.title: Final ruling: vows can be opened through regret, even by the God of Israel
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes רב נחמן: the הלכה is that a חכם may undo a vow based on regret, and he may even undo a vow made by the God of Israel.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: The הלכה is that we may open a vow through regret, and we do deal with vows made 'by the God of Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final הלכה, which goes against the strict view of רב אסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אסי refused to undo a vow by 'the God of Israel.' רב נחמן rules that such a vow can be undone like any other. He also rules that the person's regret is enough of an opening to undo the vow.

keyTerms.meaning: We open, we find an opening to undo a vow
We attend to, we deal with the request

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה follows רב נחמן: regret is a valid opening, and even a vow by the God of Israel can be undone.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not take the stories of רב אסי and רב יוסף as the final law. רב נחמן's ruling here is the הלכה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical law for undoing vows: a חכם may undo even the most solemn-sounding vow when the person truly regrets it.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rav Nachman said:
The law is: we open a vow through regret,
phrases.notes: A חכם may undo the vow simply because the person now regrets making it.

phrases.english: and we attend to a vow made by the God of Israel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: הִלְכְתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules against the strict view shown in steps 7 to 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה: a vow may be undone through regret, and even vows by the God of Israel can be undone.

steps.title: רבא praises רב סחורה, who brings a vow to רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: רבא praises his student רב סחורה to רב נחמן. רב נחמן asks to meet him. Later רב סחורה has a vow to undo and comes before רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא praised רב סחורה to רב נחמן, saying he is a great man. רב נחמן said: 'When he comes to you, bring him to me.' רב סחורה had a vow he needed undone, and he came before רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story, setting up what רב נחמן will do with רב סחורה's vow in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story connects to רב נחמן, who just ruled about undoing vows. The setup tells us who רב סחורה is and why he came to רב נחמן; the actual handling of the vow comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: To release, to undo a vow

phrases.english: Rava was praising to Rav Nachman
Rav Sechora, that he is a great man.
He said to him: When he comes to you,
bring him to me.
He had a vow to be released.
He came before Rav Nachman.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשְׁתַּבַּח לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב נַחְמָן בְּרַב סְחוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story involving רב נחמן, who just gave the ruling on undoing vows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet; this sets up the story of רב סחורה's vow before רב נחמן.

steps.title: רב נחמן keeps searching for an opening and gets upset
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks רב סחורה, again and again, whether he made his נדר with various facts in mind. Each time רב סחורה says yes. רב נחמן becomes upset and sends him away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: Did you vow with this in mind? He said: Yes. With this in mind? Yes. This happened several times. רב נחמן became upset and said to him: Go to your tent.
steps.whatsHappening: The story from the last step continues. רב נחמן tries to find a reason to undo רב סחורה's vow, but every suggestion fails, and רב נחמן gets annoyed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To undo a נדר, the חכם looks for a fact the person did not think about when he vowed. Here רב סחורה keeps saying he did have it in mind, so no opening is found. רב נחמן takes this as stubbornness and sends him away.

keyTerms.meaning: With this in mind; knowing this fact
Go to your tent; a way of sending someone away

phrases.english: He said to him: Did you vow with this in mind?
phrases.notes: רב נחמן is checking a possible fact. If רב סחורה didn't think of it, the vow could be undone.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.
With this in mind? Yes.
Several times.
Rav Nachman became upset.
He said to him: Go to your tent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun in Step 13, where רב סחורה came before רב נחמן to undo a vow.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story shows how a חכם tests possible openings, and that רב סחורה rejected every one.

steps.title: רב סחורה finds his own opening from רב נחמן's annoyance
steps.stepSummary: רב סחורה leaves and uses a teaching of רבי: a good path brings honor from other people. Since his vow led to רב נחמן being upset with him, he would not have vowed had he known this, so the vow is undone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב סחורה went out and made an opening for himself. רבי says: Which is the proper path a person should choose? Any path that brings glory to the one who does it and glory from other people. Now that רב נחמן is upset, I would not have vowed with this in mind. And he undid it for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. רב סחורה turns רב נחמן's annoyance into the very reason that undoes his vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי teaches that a proper path should bring a person honor from others. This vow brought רב סחורה the displeasure of רב נחמן, a great sage, which he never expected when he vowed. That unexpected result is a valid פתח, so the vow can be undone.

keyTerms.meaning: An opening: a reason showing the vow was made without knowing something

steps.whatToRemember: A new, unexpected result of a vow, like losing honor in the eyes of others or of a great sage, can serve as the opening to undo it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how wide a פתח can be: even the bad feelings the vow itself caused can count as something the person did not expect.

phrases.english: Rav Sechora went out
and made an opening for himself.
Rabbi says:
phrases.notes: אבות 2:1. This is רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.english: Which is the proper path
that a person should choose for himself?
Any path that is a glory to the one who does it
and brings him glory from other people.
And now that Rav Nachman became upset,
with this in mind I would not have vowed.
phrases.notes: This is רב סחורה thinking to himself.

phrases.english: And he undid it for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: נְפַק רַב סְחוֹרָה וּפְתַח פִּיתְחָא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the story: the annoyance from Step 14 becomes the opening.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An unexpected loss of honor caused by the vow is a valid פתח to undo it.

steps.title: A similar story begins with רבי שמעון ברבי
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון ברבי needs a vow undone and comes before the רבנן. They suggest openings, and each time he answers that he had it in mind. The story continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון ברבי had a vow to undo. He came before the רבנן. They said to him: Did you vow with this in mind? He said: Yes. With this in mind? Yes. This happened several times.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story that matches the pattern of רב סחורה. It is setting up an ending that comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening is told in almost the same words as the רב סחורה story: openings suggested, and each one rejected. The reader should expect the outcome to be explained next.
